Welcome to the neume workshop

This blog is for anyone who is curious : no knowledge of music, of Latin or of medieval history is required. Step by step, we are going to learn how to « read » Gregorian chant as it is written in a fascinating book, the Graduale Triplex.

Imagine a chant more than a thousand years old, handed down first by word of mouth, then written with little signs traced by hand : the neumes. These signs look nothing like our present-day notes ; they are drawings that suggest the gesture of the voice — rising, falling, lingering, bouncing. Learning to read them is rather like learning to decipher an ancient script : strange at first, then surprisingly logical.

What is this about ?

Gregorian chant, in a nutshell

Gregorian chant is the official chant of the Roman Catholic liturgy, fixed between the 8th and the 9th century. It is sung in Latin, in a single voice (we call it monodic : everyone sings the same melody) and without any instrumental accompaniment. It is a « bare » chant, entirely at the service of the sacred text. cré.

Definition — Neume

A neume is a sign noting one or more sounds sung on a single syllable. The word comes from the Greek pneuma, « breath ». A neume may be worth a single note… or a whole little spray of notes thrown out on one vowel.

Why a « triple » book ?

The Graduale Triplex (published by the abbey of Solesmes in 1979) is a chant book that superimposes three scripts for one and the same chant — hence its name « triplex », triple :

  • in the centre, modern square notation, on a staff, giving the exact pitch of every note ;
  • above, the neumes of Laon, copied from a manuscript of the 9th century ;
  • below, the neumes of St Gall, taken from other early manuscripts.

Looking at all three at once, you get both the right note (thanks to the square notation) and the way to sing it — lively, weighty, light, drawn out — thanks to the two early scripts. We shall go into all of this on the page devoted to it.

How to read this blog

If you are starting out, follow the order of the tabs : begin with The basics, then The Graduale Triplex, before tackling the six sample chants. Each chant illustrates different neumes, from the plainest to the most ornate.

To keep things concrete, we start from six famous chants : four pieces from Christmas and Easter, completed by the two Alleluias of those same Masses — enough to run through the whole palette of neumes, from the soberest to the most jubilant.

What do we mean by « Gregorian » ?

Before reading the neumes, let us go back in time. Where does this chant come from ? Why does it bear the name of a pope ? And why did an alphabet have to be invented in order to write it down ? A short history, without jargon.

1. What exactly is Gregorian chant ?

Gregorian chant is plainchant : a single melodic line, sung in unison (everyone on the same note), with no instrumental accompaniment whatever, and in Latin. No harmony, no orchestra : nothing but voices and a sacred text. This plainness is not poverty ; it is a choice, turned wholly towards prayer and towards making the words intelligible.

Definition — Plainchant

Plainchant (from the Latin cantus planus, « even chant ») is the monodic liturgical chant of the Latin Church. « Gregorian » is the name of its most widespread form, the one that established itself in the Carolingian period.

2. A misleading name : Pope Gregory

Gregory I, known as « the Great », was pope from 590 to 604. He is one of the great figures of late antiquity : a tireless reformer, the organiser of the Church of Rome, a considerable spiritual author (we owe him the Pastoral Rule and the Dialogues). Tradition also credits him with reorganising the Roman liturgy and its schola cantorum, the pope's school of singers. From there to making him the author of all the chant that bears his name was but one step… which the Middle Ages cheerfully took.

The legend of the dove

Around 873, nearly three centuries after his death, a Life of Gregory tells a scene that was to make its fortune : the pope receives the melodies directly from the Holy Spirit, in the shape of a dove perched by his ear, while he dictates them to a secretary. Medieval iconography seized on the story and repeated it endlessly : Gregory writing, the dove on his shoulder, and often a scribe spying on him from behind a curtain, astounded to see him break off… and then resume, inspired. It is this image that adorns, for instance, the frontispiece of the antiphonary of Hartker (St Gall).

What history says

It is a fine legend — but a legend. Gregory died in 604 ; yet the repertory as we know it only took shape in the 8th–9th centuries, from the meeting of Roman chant with Frankish usage (we speak of a « Romano-Frankish » synthesis). Gregory may well have set liturgical reforms in motion ; he did not « compose » these melodies, and he never saw a neume — they would appear only two and a half centuries after him.

Why the name stuck

So why « Gregorian » ? Because the attribution was useful. When the Carolingians set out to impose Roman chant on the whole of Europe (see below), there was nothing like placing it under the patronage of a prestigious pope : that gave it the authority of Rome and the prestige of sanctity. The « Gregory » label served as a seal of authenticity. The name has stuck ; the reality is more collective, later — and, let us say it, more interesting.

Key point

Gregory the Great is the symbolic patron of Gregorian chant, not its author. Remembering that is to understand that Gregorian chant is a collective work, shaped by generations of singers, and not the miraculous dictation of one man.

3. Before Charlemagne : eastern roots

Christian chant did not come out of nowhere. The very first Christians were, for the most part, Jews familiar with the chant of the synagogue (Hebrew cantillation) : for them, singing the word of God went without saying. Around the Mediterranean they were also steeped in other traditions — Byzantine, and later Arab-Muslim (Quranic cantillation) — all of which share the same reflex : the sacred word is sung, it is not simply read.

Musical examples

To listen side by side

Three pieces of listening are enough to hear the family likeness : a cantillation of the Torah (with its te'amim), a Byzantine hymn and a call to prayer (adhan), then a Gregorian psalmody for comparison.

The legacy of the synagogue : psalmody

At the heart of Gregorian chant are the psalms — those 150 poems inherited from the Hebrew Bible, sung for more than two thousand years. Christians inherited from them the practice of psalmody (singing a psalm to a simple melodic formula), but also its two great ways of doing so :

  • responsorial : a soloist sings the verses and the assembly answers with a refrain ;
  • antiphonal : two choirs answer one another in alternation — a practice the West (St Ambrose in Milan) did indeed import from the East.

More striking still : some Hebrew words passed unchanged into the mouths of Latin singers. When you hear Alleluia (from the Hebrew Hallelou-Yah, « praise the Lord »), Amen, Hosanna or Sabaoth, you are hearing a direct thread linking the synagogue to the choir of the monks.

Byzantium and the Christian East

The other great neighbour is the Byzantine world (the Greek-speaking Christian East). To it we probably owe one of the most structuring features of Gregorian chant : the organisation of the melodies into eight modes. The Byzantines had their system of eight « tones » (the oktoechos) ; the Carolingian theorists set up, in parallel, the eight modes of the West. A direct borrowing is hard to prove — but the kinship of spirit is plain.

From the East too comes a certain taste for ornament : those long vocalises on a single syllable (the melisma, see the gradual Viderunt omnes) call to mind the fervour of eastern chants. It is no accident that ensembles such as Organum (Marcel Pérès) embrace, in their performances, this colouring from the East.

One and the same gesture : the sacred word sung

Let us widen the view further : the muezzin's call to prayer (adhan), the cantillation of the Torah, Christian psalmody… three different worlds, one and the same fundamental gesture — carrying a sacred text on a melody, to engrave it in the memory and lift it above ordinary speech. Gregorian chant is one branch of that great Mediterranean tree.

A historian's caution

Talking about « influences » calls for modesty : since everything was handed down orally, we have no recording of these ancient chants. We reason by kinship and by clues (words, structures, written testimony), not by evidence of sound. So keep « family likeness » rather than « copy ».

Your question — can the scripts be compared?

Yes, and it is fascinating ! Several traditions independently invented signs « above the text » very close, in spirit, to our neumes :

  • the Hebrew te'amim (cantillation accents of the Torah) : little signs placed around the words to guide the melody — exactly the same idea of a gestural aide-mémoire ;
  • Byzantine notation (« palaeo-Byzantine » neumes), likewise at first indicating the gesture, before becoming more precise ;
  • the Arab-Muslim tradition, long essentially oral (handed down from master to disciple).

In other words : everywhere, people first memorised, then wrote down reminders — never, at the outset, a complete score.

4. The Carolingian unification

By the 8th century the Christian liturgy was everywhere in Europe… but in very different forms from one region to another : « Old Roman » chant, Gallican in Gaul, Ambrosian in Milan, Mozarabic in Spain, Beneventan in southern Italy. As everything was handed down orally, each region sang « its own way », and the melodies drifted.

Charlemagne (following his father Pepin) wanted to unify his empire — through chant as well. He imposed « Roman chant » as the standard. From the meeting of that Roman chant with Frankish usage was born the repertory we call Gregorian today. The unification was as political as it was spiritual.

5. 9th century : the invention of neumes (about 850)

One large problem remained : how to make sure that everyone sang the same thing, when nothing was written down ? The answer appeared around 850 : people began adding little signs above the text, the neumes.

Careful, this is the crucial point : these first neumes note neither the exact pitches, nor the intervals, nor a measured rhythm. They indicate only how each syllable is to be sung — rising, falling, pressing, lightening — and certain vocal effects. They are aides-mémoire : they serve to recover a melody one already knows by heart, not to discover it.

A demonstration : « Frère Jacques » in neumes

To get a real feel for this, let us play a game : here is the beginning of Frère Jacques written « in the old manner », with neumes floating above the syllables, with no staff. The dotted line stands for the gesture of the voice.

The point to take away

That is the whole logic of the first neumes : a singer who knows the melody finds his bearings in it instantly ; a beginner is left helpless. What is still missing is the information about precise pitches. That is exactly what square notation was to bring.

6. 11th century : square notation

From the 11th century onwards a decisive step was taken : the signs were aligned on a staff, which gradually settled at four lines. From then on, the height of a sign on the staff indicated the pitch of the sound. The notation does not give an absolute pitch (the choir adapts it to its voices), but it notes precisely the intervals between the notes. 7. Solesmes : the great restoration

Let us leap forward in time. Over the centuries Gregorian chant had become disfigured : melodies shortened, weighed down, « modernised » editions full of mistakes. In the 19th century a small abbey in the Sarthe was to change everything and give the chant back its authentic face : Solesmes.

Dom Guéranger and the Benedictine revival

In 1833, Dom Prosper Guéranger refounded the abbey of Saint-Pierre de Solesmes and restored there the Benedictine life, almost extinct in France after the Revolution. Passionate about the liturgy, he wanted to be done with the corrupt versions then in use and to go back to the sources : to recover the melodies as the early manuscripts had preserved them. That is the starting point of a scholarly adventure that would last more than a century.

Scholarship at the service of the chant

Two monks were to turn that intuition into a rigorous method :

  • Dom Joseph Pothier compares the manuscripts and reconstructs the melodies ; his Mélodies grégoriennes (1880), then his Liber gradualis (1883), mark the return of « true » Gregorian chant.
  • Dom André Mocquereau launches in 1889 the Paléographie Musicale : a monumental collection of photographic facsimiles of manuscripts from all over the world. By publishing side by side dozens of witnesses to the same chant, it proved, evidence in hand, what the original version had been. It is the direct ancestor of the approach of the Graduale Triplex.

The Vatican edition and the motu proprio of Pius X (1903)

The work of Solesmes received a resounding endorsement. In 1903, Pope Pius X, in his motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini, proclaimed Gregorian chant the model for all sacred music. Hard on its heels came the Vatican edition — the Kyriale (1905), the Graduale (1908) — prepared with the help of Solesmes : it is the official reference in square notation.

8. Today's performing styles

How are these melodies sung nowadays ? There is no single answer, but several schools — and that is precisely what makes listening so absorbing.

The classic « Solesmes method »

To make the chant teachable, Dom Mocquereau devised a system of rhythmic signs (little dots, episemas, « ictus ») added to the square notation. The result is the style most people have in mind : a flowing, even and serene chant, with notes of equal length grouped in twos and threes, of great purity (one thinks too of the chant of the abbey of Silos, in Spain). This was long the way taught everywhere.

From method to semiology

In the 20th century, still at Solesmes, Dom Eugène Cardine pushed the study further : he scrutinised the earliest neumes (St Gall, Laon) to read in them nuances of rhythm and expression that square notation had erased. This is Gregorian semiology — and it is exactly what gave birth to the Graduale Triplex in 1979. In other words, « Solesmes » is not frozen : the house that fixed the even version is also the one that reopened the question of nuance.

Historically informed approaches

Other artists go further still in restoring the old details, with more ornate performances, sometimes tinged with the eastern influences mentioned above. Such is the case of ensembles like Organum (Marcel Pérès) or the Ensemble Anne-Marie Deschamps (Venance Fortunat). Between the serenity of Solesmes and the exuberance of Organum there is no « good » and « bad » chant : there are two ways of bringing the same signs back to life.

Hear the difference for yourself

Each chant page brings together several performances to compare : Solesmes, Organum, the Ensemble Deschamps… Start with Puer natus est, where the monastic style of Solesmes and the approach of Organum can be heard side by side. The theory then takes on its full meaning.

A note of rigour

This blog aims at popularisation : dates and facts have been simplified for the sake of clarity. Before publishing anything, have the historical side read over with the help of the works above : research (in semiology especially) goes on evolving, and some attributions remain debated.

What to remember

Gregorian chant is a plainchant unified in the Carolingian period, with eastern roots, wrongly attributed to Gregory the Great. It was first written down in neumes (an aide-mémoire for the gesture, 9th c.), then made precise thanks to square notation on a staff (11th c.). Today several schools bring it back to life. You now have the whole context : let us move on to reading the signs themselves.

The basics : learning to see a neume

Before opening the Graduale Triplex, let us set up a few simple landmarks. By the end of this page you will recognise the Gregorian staff, its clef, and about a dozen fundamental neumes.

1. The four-line staff

Our modern staff has five lines. Gregorian chant, by contrast, is written on a staff of only four lines (the tetragram). That is enough, because Gregorian melodies move within a fairly narrow range. As today, the higher a sign sits on the staff, the higher the sound ; the lower it sits, the lower the sound. One peculiarity worth knowing : the clef can sit on different lines — it is not fixed once and for all as in modern music, and it sometimes even changes in the middle of a piece.

Definition — The clef

A clef is a marker placed at the start of a line that names one of the lines. In chant, two clefs are mainly used : the C clef (do) and the F clef . They do not fix an absolute pitch (the choir adjusts the pitch to its voices), but they show where the semitones fall, which is enough to sing in tune.

2. The basic note : the punctum

In square notation the commonest single note is the punctum — literally a « dot », drawn as a small square. A variant, the virga (« rod »), is a square extended by a small stem ; it often notes a higher note. When reading, punctum and virga are both worth a single note.

Punctum 1 note
Virga 1 note (often high)

3. Two-note neumes

Things get more complex — and more interesting — when several sounds are sung on a single syllable. They are then grouped into a single drawing. The golden rule for reading : a neume is read from bottom to top and from left to right, following the stroke.

Pes (podatus) 2 notes going up
Clivis (flexa) 2 notes going down

4. Three-note neumes

With three notes you draw small « waves ». Remember these four above all — you will meet them constantly :

Torculus low · high · low
Porrectus high · low · high
Scandicus 3 notes going up
Climacus 1 note then a descent
Memory tip

Many neume names « say » their own shape : scandicus suggests climbing (as in « escalade »), climacus going down a staircase (Greek klimax = ladder), flexa the bend downwards. Trust the shape before memorising the name.

5. Two signs that change the colour of the chant

Some small signs do not change the note, but the way it is sung. Here are two essential ones, which we shall meet again in the examples :

  • The quilisma — a note drawn as a zigzag, light and fleeting, which acts as a springboard to the next note ; traditionally the preceding note is slightly lengthened.
  • The episema — a small horizontal stroke added above (or beside) a neume to indicate that the note is settled on, broadened. It is the equivalent of a slight « leaning » of the voice.
Quilisma light note, springboard
Episema settle / broaden
Key point

A neume = a drawing read from left to right and from bottom to top. Its shape tells the movement of the voice ; a few added signs (episema, quilisma) tell the manner. You now have all the basic vocabulary needed to tackle the book that brings them together.

The Graduale Triplex : three scripts for a single chant

Why three stacked notations ? Because none of them says everything on its own. Together they give both the right note and the soul of the chant.

When the monks of Solesmes published the Graduale Triplex in 1979, they were answering an old problem. The oldest chant manuscripts (9th–11th century) are of extraordinary musical subtlety : they notate the nuances, the leanings, the impulses of the voice. But they have one major flaw : they do not give the exact pitches. Conversely, modern square notation gives precise pitches… but has lost much of those nuances. The solution ? Superimpose the two worlds.

The key word — diastematic

A notation is diastematic when the height of the signs precisely indicates the pitch of the sounds (as on a staff). It is adiastematic (or « in campo aperto », in the open field) when the signs float above the text : they show the melodic gesture without fixing the intervals. The old neumes are adiastematic ; square notation is diastematic.

The three « storeys » of the page

On a line of the Graduale Triplex, for each syllable of the text, you will find three pieces of information aligned vertically :

Above : neumes of Laon In the middle : square notation (Vatican edition) Below : neumes of St. Gall

In the middle : the square notation (the Editio Vaticana)

This is the reference layer for pitch. On its four-line staff, with its clef, it tells you exactly which note to sing. It is the one we learned in The basics. If you were to read only one layer to « get out » the melody, it would be this one.

Above : the neumes of Laon

They come from a 9th-century manuscript kept at Laon (the « manuscript 239 ») and are printed in black. This family of writing, called Messine, is famous for its rhythmic precision : it distinguishes short from long notes very finely, notably thanks to added letters (see below).

Below : the neumes of St. Gall

They come from manuscripts of the abbey of St. Gall (in present-day Switzerland), such as the Cantatorium (manuscript 359) or the Einsiedeln 121 manuscript, and are printed in red. This script is admired for the clarity with which it draws the gesture of the melody and its articulation, likewise enriched with small letters.

The « significative letters »

A delightful detail : the old copyists added small letters beside the neumes to specify the intention — rather like our markings « softly », « hold back » above a score. They are called litterae significativae. Here are some of the most frequent :

A few significative letters (usage varies between Laon and St. Gall)
LetterLatin wordMeaning for the singer
cceleriterquickly, without dragging
ttenetehold, lengthen the note
aaltiushigher (go well up)
i / iuiusum / inferiuslower
llevarelifting, lightening
mmediocritermoderately (neither too much nor too little)
eequaliterat the same pitch
How to use it in practice

There is no need to decode everything at once ! The comfortable method : first read the note in the square layer in the middle, then look above and below and ask yourself « should I press on, settle, lighten ? ». The two old layers often confirm each other — and when they diverge, that is precisely where the chant becomes fascinating to interpret.

Key point

Triplex = 3 layers. The centre (square notation) gives the notes ; Laon (on top) and St. Gall (below) give rhythm and expression. We shall now see all of that come alive in six concrete chants.

The text and its translation

Latin
English
Puer natus est nobis,
et filius datus est nobis :
A child is born to us,
and a son is given to us ;
cujus imperium super humerum ejus :
sovereignty rests upon his shoulder ;
et vocabitur nomen ejus magni consilii Angelus.
and he shall be called the Messenger of the great design.

What to look at first

Let us start gently, with the first word : Pu-er. It has two syllables, so at least two « packets » of neumes. The beauty of Gregorian chant is that a single syllable can carry several notes. Our job : for each syllable, to spot how many notes there are and which way they move.

Method in 3 steps

1) Find the syllable in the text. 2) In the middle (square notation), count the squares and follow them up and down. 3) Glance above (Laon) and below (St. Gall) : should you press on, settle, lighten ? That is all.

Syllable by syllable (start of the chant)

  • Pu- : the chant typically takes flight with a rising movement. Look here for a pes (two notes going up) — the voice « takes off ».
  • -er : the voice settles, often with a clivis (two notes going down) or a small group coming back down to the supporting note.
  • na-tus : listen to how the word « born » is brought out ; the neumes become more generous here (several notes), underlining the most important word of the sentence.
Reminder — accent and music

In chant the music follows the meaning of the text : important words (Puer, « the child ») often receive more notes or a slight leaning. This is not decorative : it is a way of proclaiming the text.

Key point for this chant

Puer natus est is a neumatic chant : small groups of 2 to 4 notes per syllable. It is the ideal training ground for recognising the pes, the clivis and the torculus without being overwhelmed. The next chant will multiply the notes…

Example 2 — Viderunt omnes

A gradual for Christmas Day, and one of the summits of Gregorian art : here a single syllable can carry dozens of notes. Welcome to the world of the melisma.

Genre
Gradual (meditative chant, after the 1st reading)
Occasion
Mass of Christmas Day
Text
Psalm 97 (98), verses 3 and 4, then verse 2
Mode
Mode V (fa mode, solemn and radiant)
Style
Melismatic : long garlands of notes per syllable
In the Triplex
p. 48

Listen to how a single syllable stretches into a long vocalise, depending on the performer.

The text and its translation

Latin
English
Viderunt omnes fines terræ
salutare Dei nostri :
All the ends of the earth have seen
the salvation of our God ;
jubilate Deo, omnis terra.
acclaim God, all the earth.
Verse Notum fecit Dominus salutare suum :
ante conspectum gentium revelavit justitiam suam.
The Lord has made known his salvation ;
in the sight of the nations he has revealed his justice.
Definition — Melisma

A melisma is a group of many notes sung on a single syllable (sometimes twenty, thirty notes or more !). It is the opposite of « syllabic » chant (one note per syllable). The melisma is the voice rejoicing, drawing out a vowel as one draws out a joy.

Why so many notes ?

A gradual is not made to be understood « word by word » like a reading : it is a chant of contemplation, entrusted to a soloist or a small, highly trained group. On key syllables — for instance the last one of om-nes or of ter-ræ — the melody blossoms into long vocalises. So do not try to « read fast » : here, one savours.

How to read a long melisma without getting lost

Faced with a garland of notes, the key is to cut it up into familiar little neumes. A melisma is never more than a sequence of bricks you already know :

  • climacus figures (a note then a descending cascade of diamonds) — very frequent in descents ;
  • linked pes and clivis figures, which make the line undulate ;
  • sometimes a quilisma, that zigzag note which serves as a springboard in the middle of an ascent.
The role of the old notations here

In such a dense melisma, the square notation in the middle shows clearly which notes follow one another. But it is above all the layers of Laon and St. Gall that rescue the performer : they show where to speed up (letter c, celeriter), where to settle (letter t, tenete, or an episema), so that the vocalise breathes instead of turning into a mush of notes.

Did you know — the jubilus

The great melisma of joy is sometimes called the jubilus, typically the one that blossoms on the final « a » of Alleluia. Saint Augustine described it as the song of a heart too full to find its words. Viderunt omnes belongs to that same family of exuberant writing.

Seeing the three notations

📜 Space for the facsimile of « Viderunt omnes »

Choose a highly ornate syllable (e.g. the melisma on -nes of omnes) and show how it breaks down into small neumes.
<img src="assets/img/viderunt-omnes.jpg" alt="Viderunt omnes in the Graduale Triplex">

Key point for this chant

Viderunt omnes illustrates the melismatic style. The right reflex : cut up the long vocalises into familiar neumes, and rely on the significative letters for the rhythm. After this feast of notes, let us return to a more intimate chant : the dawn of Christmas.

The entrance chant of the dawn Mass at Christmas. A chant of half-light, all delicacy : the perfect occasion to hear the nuances of duration.

Occasion
Mass at dawn on Christmas Day (in aurora), in the early morning of 25 December
Text
After Isaiah (Is 9, 2 and 9, 6) and psalm 92
Mode
Mode VIII (sol mode, peaceful and settled)
Style
Neumatic and measured : ideal for observing durations

Choir of the Monks of Solesmes, dir. Dom Jean Claireyoutu.be/X6Sx6K3GJOk
Venance Fortunat · Ensemble Anne-Marie Deschampsyoutu.be/laXNboqoFU0

The text and its translation

Latin
English
Lux fulgebit hodie super nos :
A light shall shine upon us today ;
quia natus est nobis Dominus :
for a Lord is born to us ;
et vocabitur Admirabilis, Deus,
Princeps pacis, Pater futuri sæculi :
and he shall be called Wonderful, God,
Prince of peace, Father of the world to come ;
cujus regni non erit finis.
and his reign shall have no end.

The real subject here : the duration of the notes

So far we have asked « how many notes ? » and « do they go up or down ? ». Lux fulgebit invites us to a subtler question : « how long does each note last ? ». For in chant, not all notes have the same duration : some are light and fleeting, others settle and broaden.

Definition — short note, lengthened note

Chant alternates short notes (the ordinary, light flow) and lengthened notes, on which the voice lingers for a moment. This is not a « square » rhythm like a military march : it is a supple breathing, guided by the meaning of the text.

Where do you read these durations ?

This is precisely the area where the old notations of the Triplex shine :

  • The episema (small stroke) above a St. Gall neume : « settle, broaden ».
  • The letter t (tenete) : « hold the note ».
  • The letter c (celeriter) : on the contrary, « pass quickly, do not lean ».
  • In the notation of Laon, the very shape of the stroke (rounded, « hooked »…) already distinguishes short from long with remarkable precision.
A very simple exercise

On the word Lux (the « light ») and then on fulgebit (« will shine »), ask yourself : does the upper layer (Laon) or the lower one (St. Gall) tell me to settle the voice, or to flow on ? You will find that the moments of leaning often fall on the words the text wants to highlight : the light, the birth, the peace.

Seeing the three notations

📜 Space for the facsimile of « Lux fulgebit »

Ideally, circle in colour the episemas and the letters t and c, to make the durations visible at a glance.
<img src="assets/img/lux-fulgebit.jpg" alt="Lux fulgebit in the Graduale Triplex">

Laon, above : the shape of the stroke tells short/long Square notation, centre : the notes St. Gall, below : episemas, letters t/c
Key point for this chant

With Lux fulgebit we move from the question « which notes ? » to the question « what duration, what leaning ? ». This is the heart of what makes the Graduale Triplex so precious : the two old layers make audible what square notation alone leaves mute.

Example 4 — Victimæ paschali laudes

The great Easter sequence. With it we change period and style : a later chant, closer to the text, and even built like a little dialogue.

Sequence (sequentia), sung before the Gospel
Occasion
Easter Day (and its octave)
Author
Attributed to Wipo of Burgundy (11th century)
Mode
Mode I (re mode, at once grave and luminous)
Style
Rather syllabic : often one note per syllable

Venance Fortunat · Ensemble Anne-Marie Deschampsyoutu.be/KFFJ7mBkdB0

The text and its translation

Latin
English
Victimæ paschali laudes
immolent Christiani.
To the paschal victim
let Christians offer their praises.
Agnus redemit oves :
Christus innocens Patri reconciliavit peccatores.
The Lamb has redeemed the sheep ;
Christ the innocent has reconciled sinners with the Father.
Mors et vita duello
conflixere mirando : dux vitæ mortuus, regnat vivus.
Death and life fought
a prodigious duel : the Lord of life, having died, reigns alive.
Question Dic nobis Maria,
quid vidisti in via ?
Tell us, Mary,
what did you see on the way ?
Answer Sepulcrum Christi viventis,
et gloriam vidi resurgentis…
The tomb of the living Christ,
and I saw the glory of the Risen One…
Scimus Christum surrexisse a mortuis vere :
tu nobis, victor Rex, miserere. Amen. Alleluia.
We know that Christ is truly risen from the dead ;
have mercy on us, victorious King. Amen. Alleluia.

What is a sequence ?

Our first three examples go back to the heart of the old Gregorian repertoire. The sequence, by contrast, is a later genre (from the 9th–11th century) and of a different spirit. It is a strophic chant : it proceeds in pairs of phrases (verses) which, two by two, share the same melody. One idea is sung, then taken up again to the same tune with a new text.

Definition — syllabic

A syllabic chant sets (most often) a single note per syllable. It is the opposite of the teeming melisma of Viderunt omnes. As a result, the text remains very intelligible — one « follows » the words easily.

What changes when reading the neumes

Good news : because the sequence is largely syllabic, the neumes are easier to spot here ! You will mostly meet isolated puncta (one note per syllable), punctuated now and then by a pes or a clivis at important joints. It is an excellent chant for consolidating what you have learned, without the density of the graduals.

Listen for : the dialogue

Find the passage « Dic nobis Maria… » (« Tell us, Mary… »). The text stages a question put to Mary Magdalene and her answer. The melody underlines this dialogue : it is a little sung theatre, almost a scene. Notice how, in this passage, the neumes stay sober so as to let the words speak.

Seeing the three notations

📜 Space for the facsimile of « Victimæ paschali laudes »

Show a pair of verses sharing the same melody : you then see the same line of neumes return beneath two different texts.
<img src="assets/img/victimae-paschalis.jpg" alt="Victimæ paschali laudes in the Graduale Triplex">

Key point for this chant

Victimæ paschali laudes illustrates the syllabic style and the strophic form of the sequence. After the abundance of the graduals, it is a return to clarity : one note, one syllable, one word — and the Easter text offering itself almost as a narrative.

Example 5 — Alleluia. Dies sanctificatus

The acclamation that precedes the Gospel on Christmas Day. A chant built on a single word — Alleluia — and on the long vocalise that prolongs it : the jubilus.

Genre
Alleluia (acclamation before the Gospel)
Occasion
Mass of Christmas Day (in die), 25 December
Text
Proper verse for Christmas : Dies sanctificatus illuxit nobis…
Mode
Mode II (low re mode, recollected)
Style
Melismatic : the word is short, the vocalise long
In the Triplex
p. 46
Listen to the chant

Watch for the return of the jubilus : it opens the chant, then comes back after the verse.

Recordings to be inserted : choose two or three contrasting interpretations, as on the previous pages.

The text and its translation

Latin
English
Alleluia.
Alleluia.
Verse Dies sanctificatus illuxit nobis :
venite gentes, et adorate Dominum :
A sanctified day has shone upon us ;
come, you nations, and adore the Lord ;
quia hodie descendit lux magna super terram.
for today a great light has come down upon the earth.
Definition — Jubilus

The jubilus is the long vocalise that prolongs the final « a » of Alleluia. Saint Augustine gives it its finest definition : the song of a heart too full to find its words. It is the melisma in its pure state — the notes no longer carry a text, but a joy.

How an Alleluia is built

An Alleluia is not a chant « in a straight line » : it is a there-and-back. The soloist launches the word Alleluia, the choir takes it up and prolongs it with the jubilus ; the soloist then sings the verse ; then everyone returns to the starting point, jubilus included. This responsorial form — a soloist, a response — is exactly the one we met in the heritage of psalmody.

What that changes for reading

  • The text is tiny (one word, then a short verse) : all the attention goes to the drawing of the neumes, not to the syllables.
  • The jubilus is read like any melisma : you cut it up into familiar neumes — pes, clivis, climacus, quilisma.
  • The return of the jubilus after the verse offers a rare opportunity : comparing the same line of neumes twice, a few centimetres apart.
The role of the old notations here

In such a long vocalise, square notation gives the notes but not the breath. It is the layers of Laon (above) and St. Gall (below) that cut the jubilus into breathable little units : a c (celeriter) to flow on, a t (tenete) or an episema to settle. Without them, the jubilus is sung flat.

Did you know — one Alleluia for several feasts

Alleluia melodies travel : one and the same melodic line often serves several verses through the liturgical year. The Alleluia repertoire is thus a wonderful field for observing the reuse of melodies — a common procedure in chant, where a known model is adapted to a new text.

Seeing the three notations

<img src="assets/img/alleluia-noel.jpg" alt="Alleluia Dies sanctificatus in the Graduale Triplex">

Laon, above : where to press on, where to settle Square notation, centre : the notes of the jubilus St. Gall, below : the gesture, the episemas
Key point for this chant

The Alleluia is the form in which the melisma becomes the subject : one word, an explosion of notes, a verse, and off we go again. Now listen to the same genre at the other great pole of the liturgical year : Easter.

Example 6 — Alleluia. Pascha nostrum

The Alleluia of Easter Day. The same form as the Christmas one, but a wholly different brilliance : the ideal occasion to compare two jubili and hear what the mode changes in a melody.

Genre
Alleluia (acclamation before the Gospel)
Occasion
Mass of Easter Day, and throughout Eastertide
Text
1st letter to the Corinthians (1 Cor 5, 7)
Mode
Mode VII (sol mode, bright and soaring)
Style
Melismatic : a brief verse, an ample vocalise
In the Triplex

Listen to the chant

Listen first to the Christmas Alleluia, then to this one : mode II gathers itself in, mode VII soars.

Recordings to be inserted : ideally the same ensemble as for the Christmas Alleluia, so that the comparison bears on the chant and not on the voices.

The text and its translation

Latin
English
Alleluia.
Alleluia.
Verse Pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus.
Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.
Reminder — the mode

The mode is the « family of notes » in which a melody moves : its resting note, its favoured degrees, its colour. Chant has eight of them. Two chants of the same form and the same length can thus produce opposite impressions : that is exactly what happens between the mode II of Christmas, grave and inward, and the Easter mode VII, luminous and rising.

Two Alleluias, the same mechanism

Go back to the previous page and set the two chants side by side : you will see the same architecture. The word Alleluia, its jubilus, a verse entrusted to the soloist, then the return of the jubilus. What Eastertide adds is breadth : the vocalise stretches further, as if the joy of Easter needed more air.

A comparison exercise

  • Count the neumes of the jubilus in both chants : the difference can be seen before it is heard.
  • Look for the resting note (the one the melody falls back to) : re for Christmas, sol for Easter.
  • Spot the quilismas : in the Easter ascents they are numerous — the voice gathers momentum.
The role of the old notations here

Now is the moment to check something amusing : across two different jubili, the significative letters come back at the same strategic places — just before an ascent, at the top of a curve, right at the end. Laon (above) and St. Gall (below) do not decorate : they articulate.

Seeing the three notations

📜 Space for the facsimile of « Alleluia. Pascha nostrum »

Ideally, place this facsimile just below the one for the Christmas Alleluia : the comparison of the two jubili then becomes immediate.
<img src="assets/img/alleluia-paques.jpg" alt="Alleluia Pascha nostrum in the Graduale Triplex">

Laon, above : the rhythm of the jubilus Square notation, centre : the notes St. Gall, below : the gesture and the leanings
Key point for this chant

With these two Alleluias you have been round all the styles : syllabic, neumatic, melismatic, and the responsorial form that sets them in dialogue. All that remains is to keep the vocabulary at hand : on to the glossary.

A short glossary of Gregorian chant

All the key words met throughout the blog, gathered here and explained in one sentence. Keep it at hand as you read.

The styles of chant

TermIn plain words
SyllabicOne note per syllable. The text stays very clear. E.g. : the sequence Victimæ paschali.
NeumaticA few notes (2 to 4) per syllable. E.g. : the introit Puer natus est.
MelismaticMany notes on a single syllable. E.g. : the gradual Viderunt omnes.
MelismaThe long garland of notes itself, sung on a vowel.
JubilusThe great melisma of joy, typically on the « a » of Alleluia.

The basic neumes

NeumeMovement of the voice
PunctumOne note (small square).
VirgaOne note (square with a stem), often higher.
Pes (podatus)Two notes going up.
Clivis (flexa)Two notes going down.
TorculusThree notes : low · high · low.
PorrectusThree notes : high · low · high.
ScandicusThree (or more) notes going up.
ClimacusOne note then a descending cascade of diamonds.

The signs of nuance

SignWhat it asks for
QuilismaA light zigzag note, a springboard to the next note ; the preceding note is slightly lengthened.
EpisemaA small stroke : the note is settled on, broadened.
Letter cceleriter — quickly, without leaning.
Letter ttenete — hold, lengthen.
Letter aaltius — higher.

The notations and the book

TermIn plain words
NeumeA sign notating one or more sounds on the same syllable (from the Greek pneuma, breath).
Staff / tetragramThe four lines on which square notation is written.
ClefA marker at the start of the line (C or F clef) that locates the semitones.
DiastematicNotation that indicates exact pitches (square notation).
AdiastematicNotation « in the open field », showing the gesture without precise pitches (the old neumes).
Litteræ significativæThe small letters added to the neumes to specify rhythm or expression.
ModeThe « family of notes » and the colour of a melody (eight modes in chant).
Graduale TriplexBook from Solesmes (1979) superimposing three notations : Laon (top), square notation (centre), St. Gall (bottom).
Laon (ms 239)9th-c. manuscript ; Messine script, famous for its rhythmic precision.
St. GallSwiss manuscripts (Cantatorium 359, Einsiedeln 121) ; a clear script for the melodic gesture.

The genres of chant encountered

GenreRole in the Mass
IntroitEntrance chant. E.g. : Puer natus est, Lux fulgebit.
GradualMeditative chant after the 1st reading. E.g. : Viderunt omnes.
SequenceStrophic chant before the Gospel, on great feasts. E.g. : Victimæ paschali laudes.
AlleluiaAcclamation before the Gospel, prolonged by the jubilus. E.g. : Dies sanctificatus, Pascha nostrum.
Going further

The best teacher remains the ear : listen to recordings of these six chants (many monasteries share them freely) while following the text, then while following the neumes. Little by little, the drawing and the sound will come together.

Bibliography & resources

A selection for going further, from the most accessible to the most specialised. Remember to check the reuse conditions before reproducing images, scores or recordings on your site.

Introductory works

  • Saulnier, Daniel. Le chant grégorien. Solesmes. A short, clear and accessible synthesis : the ideal sequel to this blog.
  • Hiley, David. Gregorian Chant. Cambridge University Press, 2009. The standard introduction in English, highly pedagogical.

Specialised works

  • Cardine, Eugène. Sémiologie grégorienne. Solesmes, 1970. The founding book on reading the old neumes (St. Gall, Laon) ; technical.
  • Apel, Willi. Gregorian Chant. Indiana University Press, 1958. A classic survey of history, genres and forms.
  • Solesmes Abbey. Paléographie Musicale (series, from 1889). Annotated manuscript facsimiles ; the origin of the modern restoration.

Chant editions

  • Solesmes Abbey. Graduale Triplex. Solesmes, 1979 — and the Offertoriale Triplex (Solesmes, 1985) for the offertories and their verses. The edition at the heart of this blog : square notation + neumes of Laon and St. Gall.
  • Solesmes Abbey. Graduale Romanum. (Vatican edition). The official gradual in square notation only.

Digitised manuscripts & online resources (freely accessible)

  • e-codices. Virtual manuscript library of Switzerland. Major witnesses from St. Gall : Cantatorium (ms 359), Hartker antiphonary (ms 390/391), and Einsiedeln 121.
  • Gallica. Digital library of the BnF. Many liturgical manuscripts, including the Laon tradition.
  • GregoBase ; Cantus Database. Databases of scores and Gregorian chants. To find, catalogue and transcribe a particular piece.
Listening

The interpretations mentioned in this blog (Solesmes, Silos, Organum / Marcel Pérès, Ensemble Anne-Marie Deschamps) are gathered, ready to compare, on each chant page — start with Puer natus est. The full historical background is in What do we mean by « Gregorian » ?
